questions.prompt: Why is code coverage described as a white-box metric?
options: Measuring it requires access to the program's source code
It is measured only from the program's inputs and outputs
It checks whether each test verifies the expected results
It is computed from the number of faults the tests detect
It can be measured without running the test suite at all
questions.explanation: Code coverage quantifies how much of the source code is executed when the test suite runs, so measuring it requires the source code; the book likewise ties coverage metrics to structural (white-box) testing. It does not check whether results are verified or count detected faults.

questions.prompt: A test suite executes every statement of a module but contains no assertions. What does the lecture say about such a suite?
options: It can reach 100% statement coverage but kills almost no mutants
It can reach 100% statement coverage and kills most mutants
It reaches 0% statement coverage because nothing is verified
It kills most mutants, but its coverage cannot be measured
Its statement coverage is capped at 50% until assertions exist
questions.explanation: Coverage shows what was executed, not what was verified, so an assertion-free suite can still reach 100%. Because nothing checks the output, it kills almost no mutants (only those that crash or hang).

questions.prompt: Consider the code if (x > 0) { y = 1; } with no else. A single test with x = 5 is run. What coverage does this test achieve for the code?
questions.explanation: The true outcome executes every statement, but an if without an else has two outcomes and the false outcome is never taken, so only 1 of 2 branch outcomes (50%) is covered. In the book's terms the test satisfies C0 (every statement) but not C1p (every predicate to each outcome).

questions.prompt: A class has 8 methods. The tests call 6 of them, and one of the called methods contains an if body that no test executes. What is the function coverage?
questions.explanation: Function coverage = functions called / total functions × 100 = 6 / 8 × 100 = 75%. Untested code inside a called method does not lower it, which is why function coverage is the weakest criterion.

questions.prompt: For the decision if (A || B || C), assume all three conditions are evaluated in every test (no short-circuit evaluation). Across all tests A takes both true and false, B is only ever true, and C is only ever false. Using the lecture's condition coverage formula, what is the condition coverage?
questions.explanation: Condition coverage = condition outcomes exercised / (2 × number of conditions) × 100 = 4 / (2 × 3) × 100 ≈ 66.7%. The four exercised outcomes are A true, A false, B true and C false.

questions.prompt: For if (A && B), with no short-circuit evaluation, the only tests are (A = true, B = false) and (A = false, B = true). Which result is correct?
options: Condition coverage is 100% and branch coverage is 50%
Condition coverage is 100% and branch coverage is 100%
Condition coverage is 50% and branch coverage is 100%
Condition coverage is 50% and branch coverage is 50%
Condition coverage is 100% and branch coverage is 0%
questions.explanation: A and B each take both values, so condition coverage is 100%, but A && B is false in both tests, so the if body never runs and only the false outcome is covered (50%). This is why 100% condition coverage does not guarantee 100% branch coverage, i.e. the book's C1p (every predicate to each outcome).

questions.prompt: When can line coverage and statement coverage give different results for the same tests?
options: When a single line contains more than one statement
When a decision contains more than one Boolean condition
When the tests execute the code but contain no assertions
When some paths through the function are infeasible
When the same function is called by more than one test
questions.explanation: Line coverage counts executable lines and statement coverage counts statements, so they differ when one line holds several statements, e.g. if (x > 0) y = 1;. Several conditions in one decision is what separates condition coverage from branch coverage instead.

questions.prompt: A loop processes a list and can run at most 10 times (max = 10). Following the loop coverage guidance, which iteration counts should the tests use?
options: 0, 5 and 10 iterations only, as equal partitions
Only 10 and 11 iterations, to check the limit
0 and 1 iterations only; multiple is optional
questions.explanation: Loop coverage requires zero, one and multiple iterations; with a known maximum you also test max − 1 and max and try max + 1, because off-by-one errors often hide at these boundaries. The book treats loops the same way, as boundary value (and robustness) testing of the loop index, and adds loop coverage to C1 to form C2.

options: Statement and branch coverage, but not condition coverage
Statement coverage only; branch coverage stays below 100%
Condition coverage, but not statement or branch coverage
Branch coverage only; statement coverage stays below 100%
questions.explanation: T1 makes the first decision true and the second false, T2 does the opposite, so every statement and all four branch outcomes are executed. The condition y > 0 is never false (in T2, x > 0 is already false so y > 0 is not even evaluated, and y = 5 would be true anyway), so condition coverage stays below 100% until a test such as T3 = (1, −1) is added.

questions.prompt: A function executes if (x > 0 && y > 0) r = 1; followed by if (x == 0) r = -1; and then returns r. Treating each if statement as one two-way decision, how many entry-to-exit paths does it have, and how many are feasible?
questions.explanation: Two independent if statements create 2^2 = 4 paths (the book's topologically possible paths), but the path that makes both decisions true needs x > 0 and x == 0 at the same time, so no input can execute it (an infeasible path). Only the 3 feasible paths count in the path coverage formula.

questions.prompt: Criterion A subsumes criterion B. Test set T1 satisfies A, and test set T2 satisfies B. Which conclusion is valid?
options: T1 also satisfies B, but T2 need not satisfy A
T2 also satisfies A, but T1 need not satisfy B
T1 and T2 each satisfy both A and B
Neither test set says anything about the other criterion
T1 and T2 must contain the same number of tests
questions.explanation: A subsumes B means every test set that satisfies A also satisfies B, so T1 satisfies B, while the converse does not hold and T2 may fail A. The subsuming criterion is the stronger one, needing more tests but giving more confidence; the book's hierarchy of coverage metrics uses the same relation.

questions.prompt: A test set reaches 100% branch (decision) coverage of a function. According to the lecture's subsumption diagram, which other criterion is then guaranteed to be at 100% as well?
questions.explanation: Branch coverage subsumes statement coverage, whereas condition and branch coverage do not subsume each other, and path, MC/DC and Condition/Decision coverage are stronger criteria above branch. The book's hierarchy agrees: All-Edges (every predicate outcome, C1) subsumes All-Nodes (every statement, C0).

questions.prompt: Each test below is written as (A, B). Which test set satisfies MC/DC for the decision if (A && B)?
questions.explanation: Going from (true, true) to (false, true) changes only A and flips the outcome, and going to (true, false) changes only B and flips it, so each condition is shown to independently affect the decision. The set (true, false), (false, true) never makes the decision true.

questions.prompt: For a decision with 4 simple conditions, MC/DC can often be achieved with how many tests, compared with the number needed for multiple condition coverage, which tries every combination of truth values?
questions.explanation: MC/DC can often be achieved with n + 1 = 5 tests, while trying every combination needs 2^n = 2^4 = 16 tests; this full truth table is what the book calls multiple condition coverage (3 simple conditions give 8 rows, so 8 test cases). MC/DC is required for the most safety-critical avionics software (DO-178C, Level A).

questions.prompt: Which pairing of tool and purpose is correct?
options: Codecov: measuring code coverage for Java
questions.explanation: PIT is the Java mutation testing tool. JaCoCo measures Java code coverage, Stryker and mutmut are mutation testing tools, and Codecov only collects and displays reports from other tools without measuring coverage itself.

questions.prompt: Which of the following is an advantage of measuring code coverage?
options: It exposes dead or unreachable code
It detects requirements that were never implemented
It shows whether each test checks its results
It directly measures the fault-detection ability of tests
It makes 100% path coverage practical for most code
questions.explanation: Coverage reveals code that no test executes, including dead or unreachable code. It cannot detect missing code or show whether results were checked, and directly measuring fault-detection ability is an advantage of mutation testing.

questions.prompt: A requirement was never implemented, yet the test suite reaches 100% statement coverage. Why does coverage not reveal this fault?
options: There is no code for the requirement, so nothing exists to cover
The missing code lies on an infeasible path, so it is excluded
Coverage tools skip code that no assertion checks
The fault is an equivalent mutant, so no test can detect it
Statement coverage counts only functions, not statements
questions.explanation: Coverage cannot detect missing code (faults of omission): if a requirement was never implemented, there is no code to cover, so the metric can be 100% while the feature is missing. The book makes the same point: specified but unprogrammed behavior is a fault of omission that structural testing cannot reveal.

questions.prompt: When code coverage becomes a target, developers may write shallow tests just to raise the number. What does the lecture call this effect?
questions.explanation: The lecture names Goodhart's law for this: once coverage is a target, shallow tests can raise the number. Faults of omission are a different limitation, namely missing code that coverage cannot detect.

questions.prompt: What is the key idea of mutation testing?
options: It tests the tests by injecting small faults they should detect
It tests the program by feeding random inputs to each function
It measures how much of the source code the tests execute
It repairs small faults in the code before testing begins
It replaces real dependencies with mutants to isolate a unit
questions.explanation: Mutation testing deliberately makes small changes (mutants) to the source code and checks whether the test suite detects them, so it tests the tests, not the program. Measuring how much code is executed is code coverage.

questions.prompt: Who first proposed mutation testing, and when?
questions.explanation: Mutation testing was first proposed by Richard Lipton in 1971; DeMillo, Lipton and Sayward formalised it later, in 1978.

questions.prompt: What is the name of the idea that tests which detect simple faults also tend to detect more complex faults made of several simple ones?
questions.explanation: The Coupling Effect says tests that detect simple faults also tend to detect complex ones. The Competent Programmer Hypothesis instead says programmers write nearly correct code, so real faults are small deviations such as < instead of <=.

questions.prompt: A mutant is run against the test suite and all tests pass. What is the correct conclusion and next step?
options: It survived; check whether it is equivalent or a test is missing
It was killed; the tests detected the change, so move on
It is stillborn; discard it and leave it out of the count
It survived; delete the tests that passed on the mutant
It was killed; merge the mutant into the original program
questions.explanation: If all tests pass, the mutant survived; a mutant is killed only when at least one test fails. The survivor is analysed (equivalent or missing test?), and new or improved tests, which must pass on the original, are added.

questions.prompt: A generated mutant does not compile. What is it called, and how is it handled?
options: A stillborn mutant; it is discarded and not counted
A stillborn mutant; it is counted as a killed mutant
An equivalent mutant; it is subtracted after inspection
A survived mutant; it reveals a weakness in the tests
A killed mutant; it raises the mutation score
questions.explanation: A mutant that does not compile is stillborn; it is discarded before counting and does not enter the mutation score. Equivalent mutants do compile but behave exactly like the original.

questions.prompt: A tool generates 120 mutants, and 20 of them do not compile. The tests kill 72 of the remaining mutants and 28 survive. Inspection shows that 10 of the survivors are equivalent. What is the mutation score according to the lecture's formula?
questions.explanation: After discarding the 20 stillborn mutants, 100 remain, so the score is 72 / (100 − 10) × 100 = 80%. The value 72% (killed / total) is what many tools report, because equivalent mutants are usually unknown.

questions.prompt: A test executes a mutated statement, and afterwards the program state differs from that of the original program. The test has no assertion on the affected output, so the mutant survives. Which RIP condition fails?
questions.explanation: Reachability (the mutated statement runs) and infection (the state differs) both hold, but propagation also requires the incorrect state to reach the output and an assertion in the test to check it.

questions.prompt: Which conditions of the RIP model does code coverage guarantee?
questions.explanation: Code coverage only guarantees that the code was executed (reachability). Killing a mutant requires reachability, infection and propagation, which is why coverage is not enough.

options: The mutant survives, because both versions give c = 3
The mutant is killed, because the constant has changed
The mutant is stillborn, because 1007 cannot be compiled
The mutant is equivalent, so no test could ever kill it
The mutant is killed, because a + b exceeds 1007
questions.explanation: With such small inputs both versions compute c = 3, so the test passes and the mutant survives. It is not equivalent: larger inputs give different results, so the choice of test data matters.

questions.prompt: A decision mutation changes if (a < b) to if (a <= b). Which test input can kill this mutant?
questions.explanation: The two decisions differ only when a == b (a < b is false, a <= b is true), so only such a test can kill the mutant; this is why boundary-value tests matter. Changing < to > would be easy to kill, since almost any test with a ≠ b detects it.

questions.prompt: A mutant is created by removing a method call from the code. Which type of mutation is this?
questions.explanation: Statement mutations delete, duplicate or replace a statement, such as removing a method call. Value mutations change constant values, and decision mutations change operators in a decision, such as < to > or && to ||.

options: Both loops run exactly ten times, so the behaviour is identical
The mutant does not compile, so it is discarded before testing
The test suite lacks an assertion that checks the value of sum
Coverage tools do not instrument the conditions of for loops
The loop body is never executed by any test in the suite
questions.explanation: This is an equivalent mutant: the code changed but the behaviour did not. Deciding equivalence is undecidable in general, so surviving mutants often have to be inspected manually, which is one of the main costs of mutation testing.

questions.prompt: Which statement about mutation testing is correct?
options: Detecting mutants is correlated with detecting real faults
It costs about one run of the test suite, like coverage
It can be applied without access to the source code
Tools can detect all equivalent mutants automatically
It is a weaker criterion than statement coverage
questions.explanation: Empirical studies show that detecting mutants is correlated with detecting real faults. Mutation testing is expensive (tests run for every mutant), needs the source code, requires manual inspection of equivalent mutants, and with suitable operators is stronger than statement and branch coverage.

The two decisions have 4 outcomes: 2000 makes the first true, 1500 makes it false and the second true, so 3 of 4 outcomes (75%) are covered. Only sales ≤ 1000, such as 900, takes the second decision's false outcome, which the book's C1p (every predicate to each outcome) also requires.

Each decision is true for x = 20 and false for x = 0, so branch coverage is 100%. Of the 2^2 = 4 paths (the book's topologically possible paths), true-then-false needs x > 10 and x ≤ 5 and is infeasible, so path coverage is 2 executed / 3 feasible ≈ 66.7%; the missing path needs 5 < x ≤ 10.

options: Statement and branch coverage are 100%, but loop coverage is not met
Statement coverage is 100%, but branch coverage is only 50%
Statement, branch and loop coverage are all fully met
Loop coverage is met, but branch coverage is only 50%
Branch coverage is 100%, but statement coverage is below 100%
questions.explanation: The loop condition is true three times and false once at the exit, so every statement and both outcomes of the while decision are executed. Loop coverage also needs zero and one iterations (n = 0 and n = 1); the book likewise separates C1 from C2 (C1 coverage + loop coverage).

questions.prompt: Each test below is written as (A, B). Which test set satisfies MC/DC for the decision if (A || B)?
questions.explanation: From (false, false) the decision is false, and changing only A or only B makes it true, so each condition is shown to independently affect the outcome with n + 1 = 3 tests. The set (true, true), (false, true), (true, false) works for &&, but for || it never makes the decision false.

questions.prompt: A catch block runs only when the database connection fails, so the coverage report shows it as never executed. Which approach does the lecture suggest for covering such code?
options: Trigger the failure with a mock, stub or fault injection
Leave the block out of the total statement count
Add more tests that use a working database connection
Measure function coverage instead of statement coverage
Treat the block as an equivalent mutant and ignore it
questions.explanation: Error-handling code is hard to cover; it often needs mocks, stubs or fault injection so that the error actually occurs during a test. Tests with a working connection never reach the catch block, and dropping the block from the count or switching to a weaker criterion only hides the gap.

Reachability holds, but with y = 2 both versions compute z = 4, so the program state after the statement does not differ and infection fails; without an infected state nothing can propagate. The mutant is not equivalent: y = 3 gives 6 versus 5 and would kill it.
